name: Chin Strap / Head Control System
keyCorrections: If they keep looking up: your hand is too shallow — dig deeper under the chin
If they keep escaping: your chest is off their back — glue your chest to their spine
If you lose the back: you released the chin strap too early — hold until you have seat belt
description: The chin strap is one of the most powerful control points in no-gi BJJ. It involves locking your hand under the opponent's chin, gripping their far lat or shoulder, and using their head as a lever to control their entire body. Systematized by John Danaher and used extensively by Gordon Ryan, the chin strap is the foundation of the front headlock ride system and a key tool for back exposure and turtle breaks.
shortInstruction: Slide your hand deep under their chin (palm up), grip their far lat or shoulder, squeeze your elbow to your ribs, lift their chin to break posture, and walk your feet in to expose the back.
summary: The chin strap gives you direct control of the opponent's head, which controls the spine, which controls the hips. By lifting and turning the head, you can break posture, expose the back, and neutralize frames. It is especially effective against turtled opponents because it removes their ability to look up and creates leverage to tip them over. Unlike a collar tie which only provides lateral control, the chin strap gives vertical and rotational control of the head and neck.
whyItWorks: Direct head control translates to spine control, which translates to hip control
Lifting the chin breaks the opponent's posture and neutralizes their frames
Removes the opponent's ability to look up when turtled — they cannot see or post
Transitions directly into back takes, rides, and submissions
commonMistakes: Gripping too shallow — the hand must be deep under the chin, not just on the jawbone
Letting the elbow flare out — keeps your arm tight to your body at all times
Pulling straight back instead of lifting up — lift the chin to break posture
Losing chest-to-back contact — creates space for the opponent to escape
Releasing the chin strap too early when circling to the back
coachingCues: Hand deep under chin, palm up, squeeze elbow to ribs
Lift the chin, don't pull it back
Chest on their spine — no daylight
Walk your feet in toward their head to expose the back
The chin strap is a handle — use it to steer their head
safetySummary: The chin strap is a dominant control position — respect your training partner's neck
Apply pressure gradually when breaking the turtle — sudden neck cranks can cause injury
When training, give partners time to tap if the position becomes uncomfortable

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Chin strap has 3 branches: Back Exposure → Turtle Break → Ride Transition

decisionTree.action: Lift the chin and walk your feet in to tip them over
Follow their hip and transition to claw ride or spiral ride
Switch from chin strap to seat belt grip and take the back

moneyDetails: The chin strap is the highest-percentage back exposure tool from front headlock
Gordon Ryan uses the chin strap to break the turtle of every ADCC opponent
Mastering the chin strap eliminates the need for complex turtle break techniques
fixItFast: If they keep looking up: dig deeper under the chin
If they keep escaping: chest to spine — close the gap
If you lose the back: hold the chin strap until seat belt is secured
